questions.question: What does the @Bean annotation on a method inside a @Configuration class do?
options: Marks the method as a web endpoint
Registers the object the method returns as a Spring bean
Makes the method run on every request
Turns the class into a repository
questions.explanation: Spring calls the method once and stores the returned object as a bean named after the method.

questions.question: When is @Bean a better choice than @Component?
options: When you own the class and it needs no set-up
When the class comes from a library and you cannot add annotations
When the class has no methods
When the class is a controller
questions.explanation: @Bean lets you create and configure objects of classes you cannot annotate yourself.

questions.question: A @Bean method named labelPrinter() returns a LabelPrinter, and no name is given in the annotation. What is the bean name?
options: LabelPrinter
labelPrinter
printer
labelPrinterBean
questions.explanation: By default the bean is named after the method.

questions.question: In a full @Configuration class, frontDesk() calls labelPrinter() directly and packingDesk(LabelPrinter p) receives it as a parameter. What does front.printer() == packing.printer() print?
options: true, because Spring returns the same bean in both cases
false, because the direct call creates a new printer
null
It fails to compile
questions.explanation: The configuration proxy returns the existing singleton, so both desks share one printer.

questions.question: A developer marks a @Configuration class as final. What happens?
options: Spring cannot subclass it to create the proxy, so startup fails
Nothing, final has no effect
The beans become prototypes
Spring removes the final keyword
questions.explanation: Full configuration classes are proxied by subclassing, which a final class does not allow.
